title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #203
gist: Packy McCormick's July 24, 2026 roundup covers Travis Kalanick's Atoms raising $1.7B from a16z to build physical industries as a vertically integrated 'computer,' Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge using Claude to disprove the decades-old Jacobian conjecture, and Skyroot's Vikram-1 making India the fourth country with a privately-built orbital rocket. It also covers a new White House science-funding reform report and Anduril/Archer's autonomous attack rotorcraft, Thunder.

themes.theme: Travis Kalanick's Atoms and the 'physical industries as a computer' thesis

insights.claim: Travis Kalanick's new company Atoms raised a $1.7 billion equity investment led by a16z, with Ben Horowitz joining the board; Uber participated in the round while Benchmark did not.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A $1.7B check with a16z's Ben Horowitz on the board signals a major bet on physical-industry roll-ups; Benchmark's conspicuous absence (Kalanick's old board adversary) is worth watching in future funding rounds.
insights.locator: (1) Travis is Back (with $1.7B from a16z)

insights.claim: In 2011, a16z nearly led Uber's Series B, but the deal fell apart and Menlo Ventures led the $32 million round instead; Kalanick and a16z frame the new Atoms investment as unfinished business from that missed deal and the 2017 boardroom fallout that pushed Kalanick out of Uber.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: a16z's willingness to 'complete' a 15-year-old missed deal shows how founder relationships can resurface as outsized late-stage checks, a pattern worth tracking with other mid-2010s founders a16z is now backing.
insights.quote: On many levels, this round is a bit of unfinished business
insights.locator: In 2011, a16z came very close to leading Uber's Series B

insights.claim: Kalanick's unifying thesis for Atoms is that physical industries can be run like a computer: manufacturing acts as the CPU that transforms raw materials, real estate is the storage layer, and transportation is the network that moves goods between locations.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This framework is the lens for evaluating every Atoms acquisition and division going forward — investors should map new deals against CPU/storage/network roles rather than treating Atoms as an unrelated conglomerate.
insights.quote: physical industries can be built like computers
insights.locator: Kalanick's unifying idea for Atoms

insights.claim: Atoms' food division (CloudKitchens for delivery-focused real estate, Otter as restaurant operating software, ProFood for large-scale food infrastructure, Picnic for office lunch delivery, and robotics unit Lab37) is the most mature part of the 'computer,' and Lab37's Bowl Builder robot can assemble up to 300 bowls per hour (200 if it also bags them) and is claimed to cut assembly labor by more than 40%.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A working, revenue-generating vertical stack (real estate + software + robotics) already deployed in restaurants gives Atoms a proof point that could be replicated in mining and transport.
insights.locator: Food is the furthest along version of Kalanick's computer

insights.claim: On the mining side, Atoms acquired Pronto, the autonomous-haulage startup founded by former Uber and Google autonomy engineer Anthony Levandowski; Pronto retrofits existing haul trucks (Caterpillar, Komatsu, and others) rather than requiring mines to buy entirely new autonomous fleets, and at Heidelberg Materials' Lake Bridgeport quarry in Texas a mixed fleet running Pronto's system autonomously hauled more than two million tons of limestone in under eight months.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A retrofit-not-replace model lowers the capex barrier for mines to adopt autonomy, which could accelerate Pronto's deployment pace versus fleet-replacement competitors.
insights.locator: Atoms acquired Pronto, the autonomous-haulage company

insights.claim: Pronto now has an agreement to deploy on more than 100 trucks across over a dozen Heidelberg Materials sites, is expanding into two more quarries this year, and just signed a partnership with Hitachi Construction Machinery; Kalanick claims autonomous haulage can improve mine productivity by 30% to 40%.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: New OEM partnerships (Hitachi) suggest Pronto is building distribution beyond its first customer, but the 30-40% productivity gain is Kalanick's own unverified claim and should be checked against independent data.
insights.locator: Pronto now has an agreement to deploy

insights.claim: The author is explicitly uncertain whether Atoms' seven operating companies will fuse into one integrated 'big computer,' remain a disconnected collection of good businesses, or collapse under their own operational complexity, but frames part of Kalanick's motivation as proving Benchmark wrong for pushing him out of Uber in 2017.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The bull case (integrated conglomerate) and bear case (disconnected businesses or collapse) are both live outcomes — investors should track whether Atoms' divisions actually share technology/data rather than just capital.
insights.quote: a desire to make Benchmark miss out on trillions of dollars in returns
insights.locator: It is yet to be seen whether he can turn

themes.theme: AI starts disproving decades-old math conjectures

insights.claim: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge, working with Anthropic's Claude model (referred to by him as 'Fable'), disproved the Jacobian conjecture, an algebraic geometry problem that had been open since it was generalized by Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A frontier AI lab's own researchers using their model to resolve an 87-year-old open problem is a concrete, checkable data point for AI's mathematical-research capability, distinct from marketing claims.
insights.quote: hello there the jacobian conjecture is false
insights.locator: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge posted the finale

insights.claim: The Jacobian conjecture holds that if a polynomial map from n-dimensional complex space to itself has a Jacobian determinant that is always the same nonzero constant (implying local reversibility everywhere), the map must also be globally reversible with a polynomial inverse; Alpöge's three-variable counterexample has a constant Jacobian determinant of -2 but sends three distinct points -- (0,0,-1/4), (1,-3/2,13/2), and (-1,3/2,13/2) -- to the same output point, (-1/4,0,0), which is impossible for an invertible map.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Understanding the actual mechanism of the counterexample (a many-to-one map masquerading as locally invertible) shows the disproof is a concrete, verifiable construction rather than a vague claim.
insights.locator: The conjecture, generalized by Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939

insights.claim: Days earlier, mathematician Dmitry Rybin used a chat session with GPT-5.6 Pro to disprove the Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture, a graph-theory problem open for about 30 years, by constructing a graph with fractional flow cost 58 where any unsplittable flow with capacity violation of 15 or less costs at least 60.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This shows the conjecture-disproving trend isn't limited to Anthropic/Claude -- OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Pro produced a comparable result independently, suggesting a broader capability step-change across frontier models, not a single-lab fluke.
insights.locator: Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture is false

insights.claim: The author's thesis is that the Jacobian disproof was 'the 4-minute mile' moment for AI-assisted conjecture-breaking -- now that it has been shown possible, mathematicians are rushing to use AI to disprove other longstanding conjectures, and he expects many more to fall soon.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If more conjectures fall in quick succession, it becomes a leading indicator of AI's usefulness in formal, verifiable domains -- watch for a cluster of similar disproofs over the following weeks as a confirming signal.
insights.quote: the Jacobian disproval was the 4-minute mile of disproving longstanding conjectures
insights.locator: Adios Dinitz-Garg-Goemans!

insights.claim: AI researcher Joscha Bach jokingly proposed a moratorium on using AI to disprove mathematical conjectures until the models are mature enough to prove new theorems instead, arguing it is much easier to destroy an existing conjecture than to build new mathematics.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A credible AI researcher framing the disprove-only capability as lopsided ('easier to destroy than to build') is a useful check against overstating current AI math capability as full theorem-proving competence.
insights.quote: We need a moratorium on using AI against math.
insights.locator: Joscha Bach (jokingly?) proposed a moratorium

themes.theme: India enters the private orbital launch club

insights.claim: Indian startup Skyroot's Vikram-1 became the country's first privately developed rocket to reach orbit, delivering customer payloads to a 450-kilometer orbit in a flight lasting about fifteen minutes.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A successful maiden orbital flight with paying customer payloads is a de-risking milestone for Skyroot commercially, not just a technical demonstration.
insights.locator: (3) India's First Private Rocket

insights.claim: Vikram-1 is 22 meters tall, can carry payloads up to 350 kilograms, and uses three solid rocket stages plus a liquid orbital-adjustment module powered by a 3D-printed engine.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: These specs place Vikram-1 in the small-satellite launch class, competing for the same customer segment as Rocket Lab's Electron and other dedicated small-launch providers.
insights.locator: Vikram-1 is 22 meters tall

insights.claim: a16z's Christian Keil described Vikram-1 as roughly equivalent in size to Rocket Lab's Electron rocket and similarly non-reusable -- a comparison to a company (Rocket Lab) the author describes as a $40 billion 'workhorse rocket' business.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If the Electron comparison holds, it implies Skyroot could pursue a similar commercial trajectory and valuation ceiling to Rocket Lab as a dedicated small-launch provider.
insights.quote: Think of it as the Indian Electron.
insights.locator: My friend Christian Keil at a16z described

insights.claim: With Skyroot's launch, India joins a very small club of countries whose private companies have independently reached orbit -- the United States, China, and (counting Rocket Lab, which first reached orbit from New Zealand in 2018 before being headquartered in the US) New Zealand -- while Russia, despite launching Sputnik in 1957 and having a decorated state space program, has never had a private company achieve the same.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The scarcity of countries with private orbital-launch capability underscores how rare this milestone is and positions India's private space sector as a genuine new node in the global launch market, unlike Russia's stalled private-space efforts.
insights.locator: India joins an even smaller club

insights.claim: Skyroot, founded by former Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) engineers, reached orbit only six years after India opened its space sector to private companies in 2020.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A six-year timeline from market liberalization to orbital launch is fast by global standards and suggests India's regulatory opening is translating quickly into commercial capability worth tracking for follow-on space startups.
insights.locator: Skyroot's speed is impressive.

themes.theme: Rebuilding the machinery of US federal science funding

insights.claim: White House science advisor Michael Kratsios released a 123-page report, 'Science: A New Golden Age,' explicitly positioned as a 2026 successor to Vannevar Bush's 1945 report 'Science: The Endless Frontier,' which originally established the federal government's role in funding basic research and led to the creation of the National Science Foundation.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A report explicitly framed as rewriting the 80-year-old foundation of US science funding signals a potential structural shift in how the ~$200B federal R&D budget gets allocated, relevant to any research-dependent sector.
insights.locator: (4) Science: A New Golden Age

insights.claim: The federal government distributes roughly $200 billion per year in R&D funding through a consensus peer-review model that is good at filtering out nonsense proposals but poor at identifying potentially revolutionary science, which often looks like nonsense before it works.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This is the report's central diagnosis: consensus-based review systematically underfunds high-variance, high-upside research, which is the exact gap that private funders (HHMI, Fast Grants, FROs) have been trying to fill.
insights.quote: It is not good at Taking Weird Ideas Seriously.
insights.locator: The federal government distributes roughly $200 billion

insights.claim: The report documents that researchers now spend nearly half their time on administrative work, that at least 270 new requirements were added to research grants between 1991 and January 2025, and that some grants take up to twenty months to move from submission to award -- almost as long as it took Boeing to move the 747 from drawing board to production.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Near-50% administrative overhead is a quantifiable drag on US research productivity that any reform proposal must address to meaningfully speed up scientific output.
insights.locator: The process has also become suffocatingly slow.

insights.claim: The report cites research showing that Howard Hughes Medical Institute's model of giving investigators about $10 million over seven years with minimal reporting requirements and tolerance for early failure produces high-impact work at nearly twice the rate of similarly accomplished federally funded peers, and it proposes applying that talent-based, long-horizon funding model at the federal level.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A nearly 2x output difference is a strong empirical case for shifting federal grants from project-based to person-based funding -- a concrete, testable policy lever worth tracking through agency implementation.
insights.locator: Howard Hughes Medical Institute provides its investigators

insights.claim: The report proposes a portfolio of new federal funding mechanisms modeled on existing experiments: 'fast grants' with few-page applications and under-a-month decisions (modeled on the Collison brothers' Covid-era Fast Grants), 'golden tickets' letting individual reviewers champion one proposal the rest of the committee dislikes, more prizes and advance market commitments that pay for results, more DARPA-style program managers, and metascience units at major agencies to test which funding mechanisms actually work.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Each mechanism (fast grants, golden tickets, prizes, DARPA-style PMs) is a distinct policy experiment; investors and researchers should watch which agencies actually pilot which mechanism as an early signal of what gets funded next.
insights.locator: Smaller, exploratory projects could receive

insights.claim: The report was released alongside an FY2028 R&D Priorities Memorandum that directs federal agencies to incorporate its recommendations into their next budget proposals and submit implementation plans within ninety days, though the report itself is not an executive order and does not immediately change how NIH or NSF award grants.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The 90-day implementation-plan deadline gives a concrete near-term date to watch for which agencies actually adopt the proposed mechanisms versus which shelve them.
insights.locator: The report is not an executive order

insights.claim: The author warns that a separate proposed OMB rule would give political appointees power to block grants before issuance and terminate existing awards that no longer align with administration priorities, cautioning this risks smuggling political control into science funding under the banner of 'metascience' and 'political accountability.'
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This is the key risk to monitor: if the OMB rule proceeds alongside the reform mechanisms, federal science funding could become more politically discretionary rather than more merit-driven, undermining the report's stated goals.
insights.quote: an obvious path from “fund high-risk work that consensus panels overlook” to “Eric Trump receives $17 billion to disprove string theory once and for all.”
insights.locator: There is a big risk here, too.

themes.theme: Autonomy extends from air combat to commercial missions

insights.claim: Anduril and Archer announced Thunder, a 'Group 5 autonomous attack rotorcraft' designed to fly ahead of human-piloted Apache helicopters as an autonomous wingman that scouts, eliminates threats, and can take fire that would otherwise be aimed at human pilots.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A named, jointly-developed autonomous attack platform between a defense-tech company (Anduril) and an eVTOL company (Archer) signals cross-sector consolidation in military autonomy worth tracking for future defense contracts.
insights.quote: The modern battlefield is a robotic kill zone.
insights.locator: (5) Anduril and Archer Bring the Thunder

insights.claim: The author's stated view is that military autonomy programs like Thunder are not a celebration of war but an attempt to reduce human casualties in what he considers an unfortunate but persistent fact of life, with an aspirational long-term outcome being autonomous machines fighting autonomous machines instead of people.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This normative framing is the lens through which the author (and likely much of the defense-tech investor base) justifies backing autonomous weapons startups -- useful context for interpreting his consistently positive coverage of defense-tech deals.
insights.quote: a way to put autonomous mass in harms way instead of humans
insights.locator: A reader commented last week that they were unsubscribing

insights.claim: Archer is separately launching a commercial version of the same autonomous rotorcraft platform, Archer Halo, targeting uncrewed missions in search and rescue, logistics, offshore energy, humanitarian and medical cargo, and maritime operations.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A dual-use strategy (military Thunder plus commercial Halo on one platform) lets Archer amortize R&D across defense and civilian revenue streams, a business-model pattern increasingly common among defense-tech/eVTOL crossovers.
insights.locator: Archer is introducing the same platform for commercial use
